title: Greek Heroes
subtitle: Excellence, cleverness, cost, and competing versions

suggestedTopics.title: Anger, honor, and consequence
suggestedTopics.description: Follow how the Iliad turns Achilles’ injured honor into a story about cost, grief, and responsibility.
suggestedTopics.prompt: Track how Achilles’ anger changes from Book 1 through Patroclus’ death and Priam’s visit.

suggestedTopics.title: Cunning, names, and disguise
suggestedTopics.description: Explore how Odysseus survives through intelligence, false names, patience, and recognition scenes.
suggestedTopics.prompt: Compare the Cyclops episode with the recognition scenes back on Ithaca.

suggestedTopics.title: When heroic stories change
suggestedTopics.description: Use later mythography and biography to see how heroic genealogies and adventures are reorganized.
suggestedTopics.prompt: Ask which source tells the version, when it was written, and what kind of work it is.

suggestedTopics.title: Heroes on the tragic stage
suggestedTopics.description: Prepare for later lessons on how Athenian drama reshapes heroic traditions into conflict, suffering, and debate.
suggestedTopics.prompt: Look for where a tragedy chooses one version and sharpens its moral or political conflict.

assessment.title: Greek Heroes assessment
assessment.prompt: Five new questions revisit the week’s events, interpretations, and source distinctions. Taking the assessment completes the week; missed answers remain practice priorities.

question.prompt: Why compare the openings of the Iliad and Odyssey?

choices.text: They prove every hero has the same ending.
They introduce different heroic problems rather than one moral template.
They are accounts of the same scene.

question.explanation: They introduce different heroic problems rather than one moral template.. Revisit the named passage and distinguish its narrative from the lesson’s interpretation.

question.prompt: Which consequence links Achilles’ quarrel to the wider war?

choices.text: It moves the war from Troy to Athens.

question.prompt: What must a return narrative address beyond travel?

question.prompt: Why keep Apollonius and Euripides distinct?
